'''Brian Halton''' (9 March 1941 – 23 February 2019) was a New Zealand [[organic chemist]]. He is noted for his investigation of highly strained and fused [[aromatic compound]]s, and was also active as an historian of chemistry.

==Early life, family and education==
Born in [[Accrington]], [[Lancashire]], England, on 9 March 1941, Halton was the only child of John Henry Halton and Mary (May) Halton (née Robinson).<ref name="Autobiography">{{cite book |url=https://www.victoria.ac.nz/scps/about/attachments/from-coronation-street-to-a-consummate-chemist.pdf |last=Halton |first=Brian |title=From Coronation Street to a consummate chemist  |page=1 |year=2011 |publisher=Brian Halton |location=Wellington|isbn=978-0-473-22319-9 |accessdate=25 February 2019}}</ref> He contracted [[bovine tuberculosis]] as a young child and consequently missed two years of his early education.<ref name="Lancashire chemists">{{cite book |url=http://researcharchive.vuw.ac.nz/xmlui/bitstream/handle/10063/4243/book.pdf |last=Halton |first=Brian |title=A legacy of Lancashire: its chemists, biochemists and industrialists |chapter=Brian Halton |pages=71–72 |year=2015 |publisher=Brian Halton |location=Wellington|isbn=978-0-473-30880-3 |accessdate=25 February 2019}}</ref> Later he attended [[St Joseph's College, Blackpool]], and [[St Joseph's Academy, Blackheath]].<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> After winning a state scholarship, Halton studied chemistry at the [[University of Southampton]], graduating [[Bachelor of Science|BSc(Hons)]] in 1963.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> He went on to complete a [[PhD]] supervised by Richard Cookson at the same institution in 1966.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> His two-part thesis was titled ''Part I: Addition reactions of a methyleneaziridine. Part II: Conformational aspects of cyclotriveratrylene derivatives''.

Halton moved to [[Wellington]], New Zealand, in 1968, and married Margaret Leach in 1970.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> The couple went on to have two children.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> In 1980, Halton became a naturalised New Zealander.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://search.ancestry.com/cgi-bin/sse.dll?indiv=try&db=NZNaturalisations&h=13631 |title=New Zealand, naturalisations, 1843–1981 |year=2010 |publisher=Ancestry.com Operations |accessdate=25 February 2019 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Academic and research career==
After two years of post-doctoral research with [[Merle Battiste]] at the [[University of Florida]], where he worked on [[Cycloalkane|small ring chemistry]], Halton was appointed as a faculty member in the Department of Chemistry at [[Victoria University of Wellington]] in 1968, eventually rising to become a full professor.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> When he retired in 2004, he was conferred the title of [[professor emeritus]].<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/>

Halton's research was centred on the synthesis and investigation of highly strained and fused aromatic compounds and their unstable [[Cyclopropanation|cyclopropanated]] derivatives, known as cycloproparenes, which included highly strained didehydrobenzenes and some exceptionally [[fluorescent]] compounds.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> in 1987, Halton was conferred with the degree of [[Doctor of Science]] by Victoria University of Wellington, on the basis of his submission of 57 papers, collectively titled ''Studies of some strained organic molecules'', published between 1971 and 1987.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://tewaharoa.victoria.ac.nz/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=64VUW_INST21131900030002386&context=L&vid=VUWNUI&search_scope=64VUW_ALL&tab=all&lang=en_NZ |title=Thesis: Studies of some strained organic molecules |date=1987 |publisher=Victoria University of Wellington |accessdate=26 January 2019}}</ref>

Halton was active in the New Zealand Institute of Chemistry (NZIC), serving as chair of the Wellington branch, editor of ''Chemistry in New Zealand'' between 2002 and 2012, and  president of the NZIC from 1986 to 1987.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> He represented New Zealand on the organising committee of Pacifichem, the international chemical congress of Pacific basin societies, for 18 years.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/>

Halton is credited with coining the name "[[ChemScrapes]]", a series of chemistry cartoons.

==Later life and death==
Following his retirement, he pursued his interest in the history of chemistry. He wrote a history of the chemistry department at Victoria University, first published in 2012, with later editions in 2014 and 2018,<ref>{{cite book | url=https://www.victoria.ac.nz/scps/about/attachments/chemistry-at-victoria-third-edition.pdf | title=Chemistry at Victoria: the Wellington university | page=147 | first=Brian | last=Halton | edition=3rd | year=2018 | isbn=978-0-475-12408-1 | publisher=Victoria University of Wellington | accessdate=16 February 2017}}</ref> and a collection of short biographies of notable chemists from Lancashire, published in 2015 as ''A legacy of Lancashire: its chemists, biochemists and industrialists''.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> He also wrote an autobiography, ''From Coronation Street to a consummate chemist'', published in 2011.<ref name="Autobiography"/>

Halton died in [[Wellington]] on 23 February 2019.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://deaths.dompost.co.nz/obituaries/dominion-post-nz/obituary.aspx?n=brian-halton&pid=191648788 | title=Brian Halton death notice | date=25 February 2019 | work=Dominion Post | accessdate=25 February 2019}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
The [[New Zealand Association of Scientists]] awarded Halton its Research Medal in 1974, and the Shorland Medal in 2001.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://scientists.org.nz/Shorland-Medal |title=Shorland Medal |year=2018 |publisher=New Zealand Association of Scientists |accessdate=25 February 2019}}</ref> In 1980, he received the ICI Medal for excellence in chemical research from the NZIC.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> Halton was elected a Fellow of the New Zealand Institute of Chemistry in 1977,<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/> and a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand]] in 1992.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/who-we-are/our-people/our-fellows/all-fellows/g-i/ |title=List of all Fellows with surnames G–I |year=2017 |publisher=Royal Society of New Zealand |accessdate=25 February 2019}}</ref> In 2005, he was awarded an honorary fellowship of the NZIC.<ref name="Lancashire chemists"/>
